newsitem.title: USA: Dollar slumps against yen but gains on mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slumps against yen but gains on mark.

text.p: The dollar slumped to its lowest level against the yen in almost four months on Monday after a senior Japanese government official said that last week's substantial yen gains against the dollar were not excessive.

The remarks from Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, sent the dollar to a low of 117.50 yen, its weakest level since mid-January.
They also sent the Japanese currency sharply higher against a host of European currencies, including the German mark, which fell sharply against the dollar as a result.
The dollar ended the day at 119.45 yen, down from 120.25 at Friday's close. It rose substantially against the broadly weak mark, ending at 1.7070 against 1.6880 on Friday.

"After a few days of selling the dollar across the board the market has had a chance to rethink and has decided that the selling against the yen is considerably more warranted than the selling against the mark and other European currencies," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer.
Last week, strong gains in Japanese stocks, talk of higher Japanese interest rates and warnings of intervention to curb yen weakness sent the dollar tumbling more than seven yen.
Sakakibara's remarks, which came on Saturday, added more fuel to the fire, sending the dollar to its low point when Asian trading began on Monday.

Efforts by Sakakibara to limit the impact of his over-the-weekend remarks and comments from a member of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party that cast doubt on prospects for a near-term hike in Japanese interest rates helped the dollar up from its lows.
Sakakibara said on Monday that the dollar was "likely to settle down soon" -- a remark traders believed was designed to limit the damage his original remarks had done.
As a result, traders began buying yen for marks instead of dollars, allowing the U.S. currency to post ample gains against the German unit and recover somewhat against the yen.
"A lot of people are talking about the disconnection of dollar/yen and dollar/Europe," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston.
In addition to its weakness against the dollar and the yen, the mark also fell against the British pound, which benefited from remarks by new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
Brown said on Monday that he had no plans to take the pound back into Europe's exchange rate mechanism, the system designed to limit currency volatility in the approach to monetary union.
Reports last week that Britain was considering joining the ERM at a rate of 2.50 marks had sent sterling sharply lower against the mark.

In other trading on Monday, the dollar settled at 1.4390 Swiss francs, up from 1.4235 on Friday. The pound ended at $1.6235, little changed from $1.6233. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3897 from C$1.3921.
